title: The instrument interviews: trombone, bass, trumpet, banjo and piano
summary: Russell lists about twenty interviews and lessons he recorded, and the planned book with a piano chapter.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So, um, I did, uh, record that Roy Palmer I got on trombone and later Kid Ory on trombone. And, uh, um, St. Cyr, of course, and Pops Foster, several bass players. Uh, uh, Ed Garland, Montuti, they call it. He was one of my very favorite musicians. He still plays in California. Well, anyway, I have about 20 interviews, uh, different instruments. Natty Dominic, um, on trumpet. Bunk would have been a logical one. He was already dead. I never did get Louie. I would have tried to get him sometime, although it's a difficult thing, the problems. Louie was very glad to talk a little bit about Jelly and interviewed him on that. But at the time I would have gotten to him, he would have been, he was gone anyway. And, uh, uh, he would never have been too interested in talking, actually, I don't think, on a thing of that kind to be published, especially. You'd have to go through Joe Glazer, which would be $2,500 or something like that, too. Like, I think when they wanted to use Louie's figure in the jazz museum, in the wax museum, not the jazz museum, the wax museum here. I think they quoted something like $2,500 to give him permission. So I just never fooled with trying to get Louie to talk about trumpet. But, uh, actually there's enough writings that you could get a lot of quotes from other interviews. Uh, Louie was widely interviewed, uh, wrote a couple of books himself and all that. But, uh, I do have a few other people. Johnny Wiggs, I had a series of lessons that he, uh, used to teach Charlie DeVore. Um, and I recorded, uh, about a dozen of those lessons. Every Sunday we'd go out and record talking about trumpet and his actual teaching there, too. So, uh, anyway, I still have that, half of the stuff isn't transcribed yet. But I still hope to get that published someday. Mm-hmm.
And this is on the New Orleans Ensemble Stock.

Yeah, it must be, uh, these, uh, I had George Gayno on, uh, who was a wonderful talker. I used to transcribe his lessons. About a dozen of his lessons, probably, on banjo. Then I got started, uh, back in the fifties, recording Mineta. He would teach all instruments. And, uh, still I have a chapter. I had Irvin Helfer, a young pianist from Chicago, recorded a lesson or two of his on piano. I would have a chapter by Mineta on the piano in the band, I guess, as they called it. That was another Otis Ferguson article called Piano in the Band, a Jess Stacy article.

And later it was a book. There was a new book, just published, I believe, on piano in the band. Is that the Ralph Sutton? Mm-hmm. They used the same title? Yeah, that's the Barge, yeah. They used the title. Mm-hmm. And I believe, uh, Dale Curran, is that his name, the, uh, guy that donated his records to two? Yeah. Did he write a Piano in the Band book, too?
That was the name of the book, I believe.

Well, anyway, Mineta would do the Piano in the Band chapter, if I ever got this book out. It might have some value, but, uh, there's been more interest in Europe, probably, and people like, uh, young English musicians, or maybe some of the Japanese might be more interested, who didn't have the real personal contact with the music, supposedly, but... Mm-hmm.
